Atomism.question: What do you know about Atomism (from Ancient Greek ἄτομον (atomon) 'uncuttable, indivisible')?
Atomism.answer: a natural philosophy proposing that the physical universe is composed of fundamental indivisible components called atoms
Atomism.fact: Atomism (from Ancient Greek ἄτομον (atomon) 'uncuttable, indivisible') is a natural philosophy proposing that the physical universe is composed of fundamental indivisible components called atoms. The concept of atomism appeared in both ancient Greek and ancient Indian philosophical traditions.

Atomism.subject: Indian Archaeology & Epigraphy
Atomism.question: He and other ancient _____ atomists argued that nature consists of two fundamental principles: atom and void
Atomism.fact: The concept of atomism appeared in both ancient Greek and ancient Indian philosophical traditions. Leucippus is the earliest figure whose commitment to Greek atomism is well attested and is usually credited with inventing Greek atomism.

Atomism.subject: Indian Archaeology & Epigraphy
Atomism.question: One proponent of this theory was the Greek philosopher _____
Atomism.fact: One proponent of this theory was the Greek philosopher Democritus.

Atomism.subject: Indian Archaeology & Epigraphy
Atomism.question: Democritus rejected _____' belief that change is an illusion
Atomism.fact: The atomistic theory aimed to remove the "distinction which the Eleatic school drew between the Absolute, or the only real existence, and the world of change around us." The views of Democritus began as a response to the work of Parmenides who had given logical arguments against the existence of change, arguing that change is a illusion. Democritus rejected Parmenides' belief that change is an illusion.

Atomism.subject: Indian Archaeology & Epigraphy
Atomism.question: They float in a vacuum, which _____ called the "void", and they vary in form, order, and posture
Atomism.fact: Democritus believed that atoms are too small for human senses to detect, that they are infinitely many, that they come in infinitely many varieties, and that they have always existed. They float in a vacuum, which Democritus called the "void", and they vary in form, order, and posture.

Atomism.subject: Indian Archaeology & Epigraphy
Atomism.question: The work of _____ survives only in secondhand reports, some of which are unreliable or conflicting
Atomism.fact: The work of Democritus survives only in secondhand reports, some of which are unreliable or conflicting. Much of the best evidence of Democritus' theory of atomism is reported by Aristotle (384–322 BCE) in his discussions of Democritus' and Plato's contrasting views on the types of indivisibles composing the natural world.

Atomism.subject: Indian Archaeology & Epigraphy
Atomism.question: On the other hand, _____'s qualitative model provided hypotheses which could be tested
Atomism.fact: Aristotle may have appeared to rejecting atomism, but in ancient Greece the atomic theories of Democritus remained "pure speculations, incapable of being put to any experimental test". On the other hand, Aristotle's qualitative model provided hypotheses which could be tested.

Atomism.subject: Indian Archaeology & Epigraphy

Atomism.fact: Kaṇāda, the founder of the Vaiśeṣika school of Indian philosophy, described atoms (paramāṇu) as eternal, indivisible, and imperceptible entities that combine to form all material substances.

Atomism.subject: Indian Archaeology & Epigraphy
Atomism.question: Kaṇāda's conception of the atom was likely independent from the similar concept among the ancient _____, because of the differences between the theories
Atomism.fact: Kaṇāda's conception of the atom was likely independent from the similar concept among the ancient Greeks, because of the differences between the theories. For example, Kaṇāda suggested that atoms as building blocks differ both qualitatively and quantitatively, while Greeks suggested that atoms differed only quantitatively but not qualitatively, and Kaṇāda claimed that the combination of three double atoms would be visible, an idea with no parallel in the greek models.
